message.content: {"name":"end_turn","parameters":{"public_message":"No builds, no deals. Liquidity first.","private_thought":"Post-roll on Park Place, cash $505, yellow monopoly undeveloped, Park Place blocks p2 dark blue. Do not build: 1-1-1 costs $450 and only pays ~$110\u2013$120; only p3 (Penn RR) can reach yellow this round (~8% on 11\u201312) so EV ~$10. Next roll from here hits light-blue hotels on 9/11/12 (~19%): Oriental/Vermont $550, Connecticut $600. Unbuilt, $505 + Park Place mortgage $175 covers $600. Built, a hotel forces selling houses at half and mortgaging the set \u2014 negative EV. Do not sell Park Place to p2: they only have $524, not enough for me to reach 3-house yellow ($1350) with a $600 buffer, and dark blue is the long-run win condition. p1 at GO has ~39% to pay p3 a hotel before building orange. Mortgage only if a debt requires it. Revisit yellow houses only after clearing light blue or if cash+mortgage still clears $600 after the build."}}
message.reasoning:
I am ready to play Monopoly as an AI player.

I am analyzing the board. I own a yellow monopoly and am at Park Place with $505 cash. Player one has a full orange monopoly and three railroads. Player two owns Boardwalk and several other properties.

Player two has partial red and green monopolies but lacks States. Player three owns a fully hotelled light blue set and holds States, Illinois, and Pennsylvania. Several spaces remain unowned: Mediterranean, Electric Company, Virginia, New York, B&O Railroad, and North Carolina.

I am reconsidering whether to build houses on my yellow monopoly. The prior plan to avoid building was based on a position at Marvin Gardens, but the current state shows I am actually at Park Place. I need to verify if this is turn 49 and reassess the risk of light blue hotel hits.

I am now choosing between ending the turn, trading, mortgaging, or building houses on my yellow monopoly.

I calculated the rent for my yellow monopoly at every house level. Three houses on all three properties would cost $1350, which exceeds my $505 cash. I cannot build three houses on the entire set.

I can only build one house on each yellow property, leaving $55 cash. I am now weighing whether to mortgage Park Place for $175 to cover a potential hotel hit from player three.

Building three houses would bankrupt me if I hit any light blue hotel. Even one house on each yellow property leaves only $510, which is still below the $600 Connecticut hotel. I am now calculating mortgage values for my yellow properties.

Mortgaging all four yellow properties would raise liquid cash to $1080, which easily covers the $600 Connecticut hotel. However, mortgaging any property in a monopoly prevents building houses and reduces rent to base rates. I will not mortgage my yellow set unless I must pay an immediate debt.

Player one is at GO and must travel around the board to reach my yellow properties, so he poses no immediate threat. Player two is at Connecticut Avenue, roughly 17 to 20 spaces away from my yellow set, meaning he could land there in a few turns but not this turn.

Player two already paid $600 rent on player three's Connecticut hotel and is now sitting on that space. Player three is at Pennsylvania Railroad, just 11 to 14 spaces from my yellow properties, so he will likely land there in one or two rolls. Player one has a full orange monopoly and can build houses for only $100 each.

Player one can build two houses on each orange property for $600, leaving $13. Two-house orange rent is roughly $200 to $220 per property.

Player one cannot yet build three houses on his orange set. He has only $613 and needs $900 for a full three-house set.

I am blocking player two's dark blue properties with my Park Place. Player three remains the most developed threat with light blue hotels.

I realized this is a post-turn action. I have already moved and landed on my own Park Place, so the immediate danger of hitting a light blue hotel is resolved. I will roll from Park Place next turn.

I mapped the spaces from Park Place. The light blue properties are nine, eleven, and twelve spaces away. Boardwalk is two spaces ahead. I will roll next turn.

I calculated the exact probability of hitting a light blue hotel on my next roll. Oriental is nine spaces away, Vermont eleven, and Connecticut twelve. The chance of rolling any of those totals is roughly nineteen percent. Boardwalk is two spaces ahead at fifty dollars. I am now mapping every possible roll outcome from Park Place.

I calculated the exact cash needed to survive a light blue hotel hit. A $550 rent on Vermont or $600 on Connecticut would leave me short by roughly $45. Mortgaging Park Place for $175 raises my liquid cash to $680, which covers either hotel and leaves about $130 or $80 remaining. Mortgaging a yellow property would also cover the debt but would break the monopoly until unmortgaged.

Building one house on each yellow property costs $450 and leaves $55 cash. A $550 hotel hit would require selling three houses for $225, mortgaging Park Place for $175, and mortgaging one yellow property for $130, totaling $585. This barely covers the rent but leaves only $35 remaining. A $600 Connecticut hotel would need an additional mortgage of $130, leaving $115. The player survives but loses all buildings and breaks the monopoly.

I am weighing whether the expected value of building houses justifies the risk. I am checking which opponent can land on my yellow properties before my next turn. Player one is at GO, roughly twenty-six to twenty-nine spaces away from my yellow set.

Player one and player two are too far away to reach my yellow properties in a single roll, so they pose no immediate threat this turn. Player three can land on Atlantic or Ventnor from Pennsylvania Railroad, but the probability is only about eight percent. Even with one house on each property, the expected rent from player three would be roughly ten dollars, which is negligible. The real danger is three houses, which would generate over eight hundred dollars in rent.

I have decided not to build houses. One house on each yellow property generates only a few dollars in expected rent, and it destroys my bankruptcy buffer against the nineteen percent chance of hitting a light blue hotel next turn. I am now considering whether to trade.

No opponent has enough spare cash to fund a three-house build. Trading Park Place for Boardwalk would give player two dark blue houses and end the game, so that is rejected. Player one already owns an orange monopoly and three railroads.

Player one has no urgent need for my properties. Player three already owns light blue hotels and lacks a complete set, but selling Park Place would not help him finish it because player two still holds Boardwalk. No opponent seems eager to trade for my yellow properties.

I considered trading away a yellow property to break my own monopoly, but that would be counterproductive. I also looked at acquiring unowned spaces or weakening other players, yet I lack the green properties needed for those trades, and no opponent is willing to trade away their light blue hotels.

I am now considering selling Park Place to player two for roughly four hundred dollars. Player two would have only about one hundred twenty-four dollars left after the purchase, which is too little to build houses on his dark blue properties. The extra cash would raise my liquid balance to nine hundred five dollars, allowing me to build two houses on each yellow property and generate over seven hundred dollars in rent.

Player two would have only about one hundred twenty-four dollars left after paying four hundred dollars for Park Place. That is too little to build a house on his dark blue properties. He would own the monopoly but remain unable to develop it, so the rent would stay manageable. The real risk is that he could collect rent and collect money from GO and then quickly build houses once he has saved enough.

Player two would need roughly twelve hundred dollars to build three houses on his dark blue properties, but after paying four hundred dollars for Park Place he would have only about one hundred twenty-four dollars left. That is several turns away. Meanwhile I could be building yellow houses instead.

Keeping Park Place as a permanent blocker prevents player two from ever completing his dark blue set. That is valuable because dark blue is the strongest set. However, player two is currently the weakest opponent. Player three's hotels and player one's orange monopoly pose a far greater immediate threat.

Mortgaging Park Place for one hundred seventy-five dollars would raise cash to six hundred eighty dollars. That still cannot afford three houses on every yellow property, but it would allow four houses total—two on one and one each on the others—with roughly eighty dollars left over. The blocker status remains intact because mortgaging does not transfer ownership.

I am now calculating the exact survival cost of building. A two-one-one house split would leave only eighty dollars liquid, and the expected rent from player three is only about ten dollars. Building would survive a hotel hit but leave me in ruins, while not building guarantees survival. The trade-off is too steep.

The expected loss from building is roughly forty-three dollars, which far exceeds the ten-dollar rent. I am now weighing whether to end my turn or trade. I am also considering how to neutralize player three's light blue hotels, though he would not sell them cheaply.

Player two only has five hundred twenty-four dollars, so he cannot pay enough to fund a full three-house build or even a two-house build plus a safety buffer. Player three would not sell his light blue hotels back to houses because that would destroy his win condition.

Selling Park Place to player two for all five hundred twenty-four dollars would leave me with one thousand twenty-nine dollars. Building two houses on each yellow property costs nine hundred dollars, leaving one hundred twenty-nine dollars liquid. The mortgage capacity of the three yellows is four hundred dollars, giving a total liquid of five hundred twenty-nine dollars. That is still below the six hundred dollars needed to survive a Connecticut hotel hit, so I would die if that space is landed on.

A one-one-one house build costs four hundred fifty dollars, leaving five hundred seventy-nine dollars. Adding the four hundred dollars in yellow mortgage capacity brings total liquid to nine hundred seventy-nine dollars. That is enough to survive a six-hundred-dollar hotel hit, but only after mortgaging one yellow property and losing the ability to build further on that set until it is unmortgaged.

Rolling nine or eleven costs five hundred fifty dollars, and rolling twelve costs six hundred. Both hits are survivable with the remaining cash, though a twelve would force mortgaging one yellow property. Income tax and the Reading Railroad are also manageable at this balance. Player two would own the dark blue monopoly with no cash to build immediately, so his rent remains low for now.

Player two could start building houses after just one or two GO turns, since each GO gives him two hundred dollars. A one-house yellow set would only yield about one hundred ten to one hundred thirty dollars in rent, which is not enough to offset a hotel hit. Keeping Park Place as a blocker is the safer choice: it preserves my intact yellow monopoly and leaves me with enough cash to survive future hotel hits by mortgaging that property.

The dark blue set is too strong to give up. Even three houses there would bankrupt every opponent, and player two could eventually build it. Selling Park Place would hand them that win condition. I cannot win faster with one-house yellows, so the best play is to keep the blocker and end my turn.

I considered trading for another color set, but completing red would require two trades and I already have yellow. Water Works is useless because the Electric Company is unowned. Player three has incomplete properties like States, Illinois, Pennsylvania, and Baltic, yet they would not pay much for Park Place since it does not complete their set.

I confirmed I rolled an eight to reach Park Place and did not pass GO. I am now considering whether to mortgage any properties preemptively.

Player one has six hundred thirteen dollars and three railroads. If he builds two houses on orange, he would have only thirteen dollars left, but that is enough to survive a yellow rent hit. A light blue hotel would bankrupt him from GO.

Player one is also in danger. From GO, rolling six lands on Oriental Avenue hotel for five hundred fifty dollars, rolling eight lands on Vermont hotel for five hundred fifty dollars, and rolling nine lands on Connecticut hotel for six hundred dollars. He has six hundred thirteen dollars, so he can pay any single hotel without mortgaging. If he builds two houses on orange first, he would have only thirteen dollars left and could not survive a hotel hit. He must decide whether to build or roll.

Player one has a thirty-nine percent chance of landing on a light blue hotel this turn. Either way, player three collects five hundred fifty to six hundred dollars. Player two is already past light blue and cannot hit it.

I will post a brief public message to avoid signaling weakness, and record the analysis for future reference. I am also double-checking the standard yellow monopoly rent schedule.

I had Ventnor Avenue and Atlantic Avenue swapped in my earlier rent calculations. The correct standard yellow monopoly schedule is now confirmed, though the conclusion remains unchanged.

Rolling doubles would allow chaining into multiple spaces, so preserving cash is even more important. I considered a trade with player two or player one to acquire cash or railroads, but neither would accept an offer that does not benefit them.

I rejected an alliance trade with player three because he is already the favorite. Player three has five hundred eighty-seven dollars and his hotels are built, so I must avoid bankruptcy while developing yellow only when safe. Building is only viable if I have enough cash to survive a six-hundred-dollar hotel hit, or if I can reach light blue after collecting more money.

I recalculated the true liquidation value after building one house on each yellow property. Selling those houses for half their purchase price yields only two hundred twenty-five dollars, so total crisis cash becomes eight hundred fifty-five dollars. That is enough to survive a six-hundred-dollar hotel hit.

The expected cost of a hotel hit is roughly two hundred twenty-five dollars in house depreciation plus the interest on two mortgaged properties. That is a steep price for the safety margin.

The expected value of building one house on each yellow property is negative. The total cost is roughly forty-four dollars in house depreciation plus thirty dollars in mortgage interest, while the only rent collected this round would be about ten dollars from player three. Player one and player two cannot land on yellow before my next turn. I will not build.
